props.title: High Sierra
props.initialSlug: Gangster's last shot at love leads to mountain doom

sections.content: **High Sierra** (1941) marks a pivotal transition in crime films, transforming Humphrey Bogart from supporting player to leading man. Director Raoul Walsh crafts a fatalistic noir that bridges 1930s gangster pictures like **Public Enemy** (1931) with the psychological complexity of film noir. The story of Roy Earle, an aging criminal facing his last job, established the "doomed criminal" template that influenced everything from White Heat (1949) to **Dog Day Afternoon** (1975). John Huston and W.R. Burnett's screenplay infuses surprising humanity into what could've been a standard crime tale.

sections.content: The film's location shooting in California's Sierra Nevada mountains revolutionized crime films, moving them out of studio backlots into stark natural environments. This visual approach influenced **Gun Crazy** (1950) and **Thieves' Highway** (1949), establishing a grittier, more realistic aesthetic. Ida Lupino's performance as Marie showcases the complex female characters emerging in noir, moving beyond simple gangster's-moll stereotypes.

**High Sierra** (1941) also pioneered the "last job gone wrong" narrative that became a noir staple. This influenced classics like The Asphalt Jungle (1950) and **The Killing** (1956), where elaborate heists inevitably unravel. The film's tragic ending on Mount Whitney set a template for noir's fascination with dramatic final standoffs, seen later in White Heat (1949) and **The Third Man** (1949). sections.content: Roy Earle's psychological complexity marked a significant shift from earlier gangster films. Unlike the brash, violent protagonists of **Little Caesar** (1931) or **Scarface** (1932), Earle is contemplative and world-weary. This characterization influenced later noir antiheroes like those in **Out of the Past** (1947) and **Criss Cross** (1949). The film's emphasis on fate and inevitable doom became central to noir's philosophical outlook.
